# Part 6: Daemon / Session-Mode Architecture

> **Status: research-backed design, not yet implemented.** Nothing in this file is required for
> v0.1.0. It exists so that when daemon/session work actually starts — for `ra_ap_hir`, Salsa,
> `jdtls`, Kotlin/Scala full semantic resolution, or any of the other real-compiler-frontend tiers
> from [05-research-and-decisions.md §12](./05-research-and-decisions.md) — it slots into an
> already-considered shape instead of forcing a rewrite of `LanguageAnalyzer`/`AnalyzerRegistry`/
> the cache layer. Validated by a 16-agent research pass (9 per-language backends, 3 cross-cutting
> architecture questions, 3 adversarial critiques, one synthesis) — see
> [05-research-and-decisions.md §14](./05-research-and-decisions.md) for how that research was run
> and where its sources live.

Part of the [monokl spec](./README.md).

## 1. Why this exists

monokl has no daemon by default — every invocation is a fresh process reading from an on-disk
cache. Real semantic resolution (name/type resolution, cross-file reference correctness) for
several languages needs a real compiler/language-server backend holding live project state, which
is fundamentally incompatible with "fresh process per invocation." That's `CapabilityPrecision::
Exact`, and it's been deliberately deferred rather than built into the default path.

The risk this file addresses: deferring a decision isn't the same as having no opinion on its
shape. If the eventual daemon design doesn't fit how `LanguageAnalyzer`/`AnalyzerRegistry` already
work, "add the daemon later" becomes "rewrite the core traits later." This file is that shape,
stress-tested against how real backends for every language monokl targets actually behave — not
invented in the abstract.

## 2. The `PrecisionUpgrader` trait

A second trait, separate from `LanguageAnalyzer`, sitting alongside `AnalyzerRegistry`: it takes an
already-produced result from the base per-file analysis and optionally enriches it using an
external resource (a real compiler or language server). It never runs instead of `LanguageAnalyzer`
— only after, and only when available.

The original sketch of this trait proposed `upgrade() -> Result<CapabilityPrecision>`: promote a
bare precision tier and nothing else. **The research found this wrong, independently, in five
separate per-language studies** — Kotlin, Go, Scala, Rust, and C++ each produce real backend output
that doesn't fit "one precision tier, promoted":

- **Kotlin**'s `KaCallInfo` is a sealed type: ambiguous resolution isn't a lower-confidence single
  answer, it's `KaErrorCallInfo { candidateCalls: Vec<KaCall>, diagnostic }` — a genuine set of
  candidates plus a reason. Forcing this into "promoted to Exact" or "left at Heuristic" destroys
  exactly the information that makes it useful to an agent.
- **Go**'s `gopls` runs two distinct, never-unified algorithms for interface satisfaction — a
  local, real-`go/types`-assignability check, and a global, method-set-fingerprint approximation.
  It never collapses these into one verdict; monokl shouldn't either.
- **Scala**'s Metals can hand back a resolved implicit value without correctly explaining *why* it
  won (a documented, open Metals bug conflates attribution) — this is two independently-scored
  axes, resolved-value precision and reasoning/provenance precision, not one.
- **Rust**'s `ra_ap_hir` and **C++**'s Clang `RecoveryExpr` both surface genuinely new structured
  facts (trait predicates and dyn-compatibility violations; preserved partial subexpressions after
  a semantic error) that don't fit a precision bump at all — they're real data, not a confidence
  signal on existing data.

**Fix**: `upgrade()` returns an outcome that carries (a) a possibly-partial precision tier, (b) an
additive, per-language-typed extension payload (§4), and (c) room for multiple ranked or ambiguous
candidates rather than one collapsed answer. This is a correctness requirement, not a nice-to-have
— collapsing Kotlin's candidate set or Go's confirmed/candidate split into one enum value
manufactures false confidence the upstream tool never claimed.

```rust
pub trait PrecisionUpgrader: Send + Sync {
    fn languages(&self) -> &[LanguageId];
    /// Cheap, synchronous check — toolchain present, session reachable. Never blocks on a
    /// full backend init.
    fn is_available(&self) -> bool;
    fn upgrade(&self, request: UpgradeRequest) -> Result<UpgradeOutcome>;
}

pub struct UpgradeOutcome {
    /// What this specific upgrade attempt actually achieved — may still be `Heuristic`/
    /// `Structural` if a sentinel (§5) indicated the backend degraded internally.
    pub precision: CapabilityPrecision,
    /// Which backend/operation produced this, for provenance — see §5 rule 5.
    pub provenance: &'static str,
    /// Zero, one, or many candidates. A single confident answer is `candidates.len() == 1`;
    /// an ambiguous result (Kotlin overload resolution, Go interface satisfaction) is
    /// `candidates.len() > 1` with no candidate silently dropped.
    pub candidates: Vec<UpgradeCandidate>,
    /// Real, per-language-typed data this backend exposed that has no generic shape —
    /// never flattened. See §4.
    pub extension: Option<DaemonExtension>,
}
```

## 3. Lifetime: a property of each resource, not one field per implementation

The original sketch had one `lifetime` field per `PrecisionUpgrader` impl: `PerCall` (spawn fresh,
use once, discard), `PerInvocation` (constructed once, reused across one CLI run), `Session`
(reserved — held warm across many calls within whatever process embeds monokl for a while).

**The duration axis itself survived unchanged** — every backend researched maps cleanly onto one
of the three as a *ceiling* on how cheap a call can afford to be. No language demanded a fourth
duration tier. But two refinements are required, both found by adversarial critique against real
backend behavior rather than nitpicking the design in the abstract:

**(a) Lifetimes nest.** rust-analyzer's own `proc-macro-srv-cli` is a subprocess "loaded once and
reused for many expansions with crash-supervision" — living *inside* an otherwise-`PerInvocation`
Salsa database build. A flat `lifetime: PerInvocation` on `RustUpgrader` can't express "this
upgrader also owns a nested, supervised sub-resource with its own restart lifecycle." C++ shows the
same pattern from the other direction: `ClangAstUpgrader{PerCall}` and `ClangdUpgrader{Session}`
end up as two separate trait impls for one language because a single impl can't honestly carry two
lifetimes. Fix: an upgrader declares a *set* of typed sub-resources, each with its own lifetime,
rather than being forced into one lifetime bucket.

**(b) `Session` must distinguish owned vs. attached.** The original framing — "held warm across
calls within whatever process embeds monokl" — implies monokl (or its host) spawns and owns the
resource. Real production models don't always work that way: `gopls`'s actual deployment is
`-remote=auto`, discovering and attaching to a daemon that may already be running, spawned by an
entirely different process, with its own independent restart/versioning lifecycle monokl has no
control over. `kotlin-lsp`'s RocksDB-backed on-disk index persistence exists for the same reason —
surviving across processes that don't share ownership. "Spawn and own" vs. "discover, attach, and
version-check a resource owned elsewhere" are different failure surfaces (stale daemon, version
mismatch, no daemon present, socket permissions) that one `Session` variant doesn't name.

Neither refinement is a fork of the trait. Both are refinements to the enum's granularity:

```rust
pub enum ResourceLifetime {
    PerCall,
    PerInvocation,
    Session(SessionOwnership),
}

pub enum SessionOwnership {
    /// monokl's host process spawns and fully owns this resource.
    Owned,
    /// monokl discovers and attaches to a resource it doesn't control the lifecycle of —
    /// must detect absence, staleness, and version mismatch rather than assume presence.
    Attached,
}
```

**Concurrency contract, required regardless of ownership**: `WorkspaceIndex::build` already
parallelizes per-file analysis (`par_iter`). A naive `Arc<Mutex<ChildProcess>>` `Session` resource
sharing one stdio pipe across worker threads is not just slow but actively wrong — concurrent
writes/reads on one pipe can cross-wire which response belongs to which request. Real precedent
(rust-analyzer's `GlobalState`/Salsa snapshot model, gopls's Session→View→Snapshot hierarchy) is
**not** a single-threaded actor — both allow real read concurrency by never exposing raw mutable
shared state, instead cloning `Arc`s into an immutable snapshot per request. Contract: every
`Session` resource must be a `Send + Sync` handle, primed/loaded in a single-threaded phase before
being handed to parallel readers, with LSP-speaking backends specifically wrapped in a
connection-actor (one task owns stdio, demultiplexes by request ID — the standard pattern
`async-lsp`/`tower-lsp`-style clients already implement, not something monokl invents from
scratch). For an in-process Rust `Session` built directly on `ra_ap_ide`'s Salsa `RootDatabase`,
this contract has a sharp edge: any lazy `set_file_text`-style write during parallel analysis bumps
Salsa's revision counter and cancels every other in-flight query against that database. All Salsa
inputs must be loaded in a single-threaded prime phase before the database is handed to parallel
readers; `PrecisionUpgrader::upgrade` itself must be read-only against the resource.

## 4. Ingestion model: `DaemonExtension`, additive and per-language

monokl's existing shared-envelope/per-language-variant pattern (`FileAnalysis` → `LangData::
{TypeScript, Rust, ...}`) already matches the strongest real precedent found for this exact
problem — three independent, decades-refined systems converge on the same answer:

- **SCIP**'s `SymbolInformation.kind` is one enum, but explicitly enumerates dozens of
  language-tailored variants (`AbstractMethod` for Java/Kotlin, `PureVirtualMethod` for C++,
  `Accessor`/`SingletonClass` for Ruby) rather than collapsing to one generic "callable" — its own
  spec states the rationale plainly: a Java method and a Go function get different `kind`s "even
  if the symbols for these use the same syntax for the descriptor."
- **LSP**'s extension model reserves vendor-namespaced methods for anything a specific server needs
  beyond its ~18-feature generic baseline, with an explicit compatibility rule: clients ignore
  capabilities they don't understand, and enum values are versioned so the consuming side "should
  simply ignore" a value it doesn't recognize. Absence degrades silently by design.
- **CodeQL** ships a `shared/` tree of language-agnostic frameworks (dataflow, SSA, type-inference)
  that each per-language library (Java, C++, Python, Rust, ...) implements concretely — shared base
  predicates plus one full schema per language, never a universal schema.

All three reject lowest-common-denominator collapse in favor of typed per-language leaves inside a
shared structural envelope. But daemon-tier data is structurally different from what `LangData`
already models: it's an optional, resource-gated *enrichment pass* over an already-complete base
result, produced independently of and later than the base analyzer — not a peer data source. None
of the three precedents has this "upgrade pass" shape natively (SCIP documents, CodeQL databases,
and LSP capability sets are each produced once, in one pass). The transferable mechanism is LSP's
capability-negotiation pattern specifically:

```rust
pub struct FileAnalysis {
    // ...existing fields unchanged...
    pub language_data: LangData,
    /// Present only when a PrecisionUpgrader actually ran and produced a result. Absence is
    /// safe and silent — no upgrader ran, Session wasn't available, or the project was gated
    /// by size (see Java, §5). Never merged into `language_data`.
    pub daemon_extension: Option<DaemonExtension>,
}

pub enum DaemonExtension {
    Rust(RustTraitFacts),
    Go(GoSatisfactionFacts),
    Java(JavaClasspathFacts),
    Kotlin(KotlinSmartCastFacts),
    Scala(ScalaImplicitFacts),
    Cpp(CppRecoveryFacts),
    // ... one variant per language that ships a PrecisionUpgrader, added as each lands.
}

/// Go's gopls never unifies its local (real go/types assignability) and global
/// (method-set-fingerprint) interface-satisfaction algorithms into one verdict — neither
/// should monokl.
pub struct GoSatisfactionFacts {
    pub confirmed: Vec<SymbolRef>,
    pub candidate: Vec<SymbolRef>,
}

/// Metals can supply the resolved implicit value without reliably explaining why it won
/// (a documented, open Metals attribution bug) — these are two independently-scored axes.
pub struct ScalaImplicitFacts {
    pub resolved_value: CapabilityPrecision,
    pub provenance: CapabilityPrecision,
}
```

`CapabilityPrecision` stays exactly what it already is — the base analyzer's own honest self-report
— and is untouched by whether a `daemon_extension` is present. The extension is additive
provenance, not a replacement value. `TraitImplIndex`-style per-language indexes remain the natural
home for language-specific facts inside each extension variant; this doesn't invent a new generic
index type, it gives daemon-sourced facts the same kind of home hand-rolled heuristic facts already
have.

## 5. Confidence-signaling rules

The single most direct finding for monokl's stated priority — correct, high-quality data an agent
won't be misled by, not uniform data. **Neither LSP nor SCIP has a confidence field**, verified by
direct inspection of both specs: `Location`/`LocationLink` carry only position; `ResponseError`
carries only `code`/`message`/`data`; SCIP's `Relationship`/`Occurrence` messages carry none either.
A server that resolved unambiguously and a server that guessed produce byte-identical response
shapes. This is a real, structural gap in the wire formats monokl's daemon tier will talk to — not
something monokl can query its way around.

The important nuance: **the compilers themselves often do know — the protocol is what throws it
away.** Verified directly in source, three real, queryable internal signals exist that never reach
a plain LSP response:

- **Clang**: `RecoveryExpr` is a real AST node Clang emits when it can't resolve an overload, call,
  or type — "acts as a placeholder to maintain the rough structure of the parsing tree... but [has]
  no language semantics attached." The compiler knows. `textDocument/hover` doesn't say so; clangd
  emits whatever type string it has. The signal survives only through clangd's non-standard
  `textDocument/ast` extension (`ASTNode.kind`/`role`/`arcana`), not plain LSP.
- **Eclipse JDT**: `IBinding.isRecovered()` — verified against `eclipse-jdt/eclipse.jdt.core`
  source — is set whenever classpath gaps or unresolved types force JDT to fabricate a placeholder
  binding. It exists on JDT's Core DOM API. `jdtls`'s LSP surface doesn't expose it per-symbol; the
  only user-facing signal is a project-level "classpath is incomplete" warning, too coarse to say
  which specific reference silently degraded.
- **TypeScript**: the checker internally distinguishes a genuine `any` from an unresolved/error
  type, but the language service collapses both to the literal string `"any"` in hover output — the
  wire-level answer is indistinguishable from a deliberate `any`. The one honest signal
  (implicit-any suggestion diagnostics) lives in a separate, opt-in diagnostic category monokl would
  have to deliberately request and correlate by span.

The common pattern: each resolver has an internal escape-hatch representation for "I couldn't
really solve this" (a dependent/recovery type, a recovered-binding flag, a platform-type marker, a
silently-first-picked candidate), and in every case that escape hatch is a small, enumerable,
tool-specific sentinel — not a diagnostic that generically propagates through LSP. That
enumerability is what makes generic detection possible: monokl doesn't need per-language semantic
understanding here, it needs a per-backend denylist of sentinel shapes.

**Actionable rules, required before any `PrecisionUpgrader` promotes a result toward `Exact`**:

1. **Never trust protocol silence.** A missing `ResponseError` or absent diagnostic proves nothing
   — LSP has no wire-level field for "resolved to a degraded fallback."
2. **Prefer native/extended APIs that expose the backend's own confidence bit** over plain LSP:
   JDT `IBinding.isRecovered()`, Kotlin's `KaErrorCallInfo` sealed type, clangd's `textDocument/ast`
   extension, TS's separate opt-in suggestion-diagnostics channel. Plain LSP structurally cannot
   carry these signals even when the compiler computed them internally.
3. **Maintain a per-backend sentinel denylist**, checked on every promotion attempt: JDT
   `isRecovered() == true`; Clang dependent/recovery type strings or diagnostics at or upstream of
   the queried span; TS hover text of bare `any` not matching an explicit source annotation
   (diffable against OXC's own Heuristic-tier read of the source); Kotlin `T!` platform-type
   markers or `SMARTCAST_IMPOSSIBLE`; Scala ambiguous-implicit compiler notices; Go's
   global-algorithm-only matches (cap those at `candidate`, never `confirmed` — see §4's
   `GoSatisfactionFacts`).
4. **When only generic LSP is available and no sentinel exists**, cap at `Structural` if the file
   has any diagnostic at or upstream of the queried location, and emit a monokl `Diagnostic`
   explaining the downgrade rather than guessing.
5. **Tag every upgraded result with backend + operation identity** — "Exact via JDT full
   resolution" vs. "Exact via clangd without `compile_commands.json`" — never an undifferentiated
   `Exact` bucket. This mirrors the CHA/RTA/points-to literature's own discipline
   ([05-research-and-decisions.md §8](./05-research-and-decisions.md)): an analysis tier is carried
   as metadata and never erased, so a consumer can reason differently about a CHA-derived edge than
   a points-to-derived one. The `UpgradeOutcome.provenance` field in §2 is this tag.

## 6. Per-language lifetime table

Real backend, real lifetime fit, and — critically — what's genuinely language-specific and must
not be flattened into the shared `DaemonExtension` shape.

| Language | Real backend | Lifetime | What must not be flattened |
|---|---|---|---|
| TypeScript/JS | tsserver / `typescript-go` (TS 7.0's LSP server, GA July 2026) | `PerCall` unusable — cost is whole-program graph construction, not per-query; `PerInvocation` a viable but costly stopgap; `Session` is the tool's **native** operating mode (VS Code never runs it any other way) | Genuine `any` vs. gave-up-and-defaulted-to-`any` — invisible unless the separate opt-in suggestion-diagnostics channel is deliberately correlated by span |
| Rust | `ra_ap_hir` / Salsa | `PerInvocation` (fresh Salsa DB still memoizes across one run — confirmed by rust-analyzer's own `analysis-stats` subcommand) as near-term default; `Session` matches the real `GlobalState`/VFS/snapshot design; a nested `PerCall`/`Session` proc-macro-server sub-resource lives inside either | Trait predicates, dyn-compatibility violations (`PredicateEvaluationResult`/`DynCompatibilityViolation`), generic monomorphization — real trait-solver output, not string/AST matching |
| Python | Pyrefly / `ty` | Both are Rust-*implemented* but subprocess/LSP-*integrated* — neither ships an embeddable Rust library API today, so "Rust-native" doesn't mean "in-process." `PerInvocation` works; `Session` is where their Salsa/incremental advantage actually pays off | The categorical `Any`/`Unknown` distinction (gradual typing's own uncertainty marker) — map directly, don't invent a scalar confidence score no upstream tool provides |
| Go | `gopls` | `PerCall` untenable (cold start documented at 10s–3m26s+); `PerInvocation` only marginal; `Session, Attached` — a thin forwarder to gopls's own `-remote=auto` daemon, not monokl-owned | Confirmed (local, real `go/types` assignability) vs. candidate (global method-set-fingerprint) interface satisfaction — gopls itself never unifies these, see `GoSatisfactionFacts` (§4) |
| Java | `jdtls` / JDT Core | `PerCall` non-viable; `PerInvocation` **fragile, not safe as default** — batched Maven import OOM-crashes past ~3000 files, a hard crash, not a graceful slowdown; `Session` is the only lifetime that amortizes both cold-start and import cost, and needs an explicit project-size gate before attempting promotion at all | `IBinding.isRecovered()` — a real, queryable "this is a fabricated placeholder" flag on JDT's Core API, not exposed through `jdtls`'s LSP surface |
| Kotlin | `kotlin-lsp` (full IntelliJ, Alpha) or standalone Analysis API (explicitly unstable per JetBrains' own docs, unchanged since first checked) | `PerCall` ruled out (GB-scale allocation, seconds-to-minutes even for a single init); `Session` **with a recycling/health contract** — bounded by staleness or memory budget, since unbounded warm sessions leak per JetBrains' own tracker | `KaErrorCallInfo{candidateCalls, diagnostic}` ambiguity, `SMARTCAST_IMPOSSIBLE` diagnostics, flexible/platform types (`T!`) — first-class sealed/typed signals, map to `candidates`/extension fields, never a binary |
| Scala | Metals (`mtags` + Build Server Protocol + presentation compiler) | `PerCall`/`PerInvocation` both repay a 10s–15min build import; **`Session`-only in practice**. BSP is fully internal to Metals — not a second protocol monokl needs to speak | Implicit argument/conversion resolution as two independently-scored axes (resolved value vs. provenance) — see `ScalaImplicitFacts` (§4); Metals can be confidently wrong about *why*, not just silent |
| C/C++ | Clang subprocess (`clang-ast`) **and** clangd, as **two separate `PrecisionUpgrader` impls** | `PerCall`: `clang-ast`, genuinely cheap per translation unit; `Session`: clangd's background index, hours-scale cold start on large projects, only viable warm | `RecoveryExpr`'s preserved partial subexpressions/dependent types — carry as `CppRecoveryFacts` extension, never collapsed into a precision bump |
| C# | Roslyn (OmniSharp / `csharp-ls` / Microsoft's own server) | `PerInvocation`/`Session`, standard workspace-load-then-reuse, no architectural surprise | Not deeply differentiated by this research round — verify Microsoft's official server's redistribution/licensing terms outside VS Code before depending on it |
| Ruby | Sorbet (near-zero fixed cold start via a compiled-in stdlib blob) or Solargraph | **`PerCall` is genuinely viable for Sorbet** — the one real exception found to "PerCall is a trap" for a real semantic backend | The fixed-cost floor is uniquely cheap; project-size-proportional check time still applies on top of it, don't oversell the headline number |
| PHP | Intelephense | `PerInvocation`/`Session`, standard shape | Licensing (proprietary premium tier), not architecture, is the real constraint |

## 7. Genuinely uncertain — not papered over

- No rigorous published data exists on what fraction of Java symbol references are
  external-JAR-only; a bytecode-LOC statistic found during research measures a different thing and
  shouldn't be repurposed as a reference-density estimate.
- Microsoft's official C# language server's redistribution/licensing terms outside VS Code were
  not confirmed.
- `ra_ap_hir`'s public API surfaces no explicit "multiple equally-valid candidates" variant for
  trait-method ambiguity, unlike Kotlin's `KaErrorCallInfo` — this may be a real gap in
  `ra_ap_hir` itself, not just something this research round didn't find.
- TS 7.0's promised embeddable programmatic API (targeted for 7.1) doesn't exist yet — today's
  integration must go through LSP JSON-RPC only. Revisit the TypeScript row above once 7.1 ships.
- Sourcegraph's own historical live-language-server-then-pivot-to-SCIP narrative was not
  independently re-verified against a primary source this round — treat it as background context,
  not a confirmed fact this file relies on.
- Whether `SessionOwnership`'s owned-vs-attached split needs to be a full enum variant or could
  stay a lighter metadata flag on `Session` was not stress-tested against an actual implementation.

## 8. What's confirmed, unchanged

Worth stating plainly since it's easy to read a file full of amendments as "the original idea was
wrong": the core shape survived real, adversarial, per-language scrutiny. Every backend researched
maps onto `PerCall`/`PerInvocation`/`Session` as a real ceiling on affordable call frequency — no
language demanded a fourth duration tier. `FileAnalysis`/`LangData`'s existing shared-envelope,
per-language-variant pattern is confirmed, not replaced, as the right template — `DaemonExtension`
extends it additively rather than requiring a redesign. And a generic Rust LSP client
(`lsp-server`/`async-lsp`, following Helix's `helix-lsp` as real, verified precedent for one client
driving rust-analyzer/gopls/clangd/pyright/jdtls uniformly) is a legitimate way to implement the
transport for every LSP-speaking backend — it just doesn't unify the non-LSP tiers (Clang
subprocess, JVM subprocess) already decided in §12, which stay separate implementations of the
same `PrecisionUpgrader` trait.

## 14. Daemon/session-mode architecture — moved to Part 6

The open daemon/session-mode question (§4) got a dedicated, research-backed design pass: a
16-agent workflow (9 per-language backend studies — TypeScript, Rust, Python, Go, Java, Kotlin,
Scala, C/C++, and a combined C#/Ruby/PHP pass — 3 cross-cutting architecture questions, 3
adversarial critiques of a draft design, and one synthesis) stress-tested a proposed
`PrecisionUpgrader` trait against how real semantic backends for every language on this roadmap
actually behave, rather than designing it in the abstract. The result is substantial enough to
need its own file rather than another entry here, per this log's own convention for
substantial changes: see **[06-daemon-architecture.md](./06-daemon-architecture.md)** for the full
design — the trait shape, the lifetime model (and why it needs to nest and distinguish
owned-vs-attached), the `DaemonExtension` ingestion model, confidence-signaling rules, and the
per-language lifetime table.

`PerInvocation`/`Session` as a real cost ceiling, no language demanded a fourth tier), but the
trait's *return type* did not — five independent per-language studies (Kotlin, Go, Scala, Rust,
C++) converged on the same finding that "promote a bare `CapabilityPrecision`" destroys real
candidate sets, dual precision axes, and structured facts the underlying tools actually hand back.
Also produced: real backend identification per language (`typescript-go`/TS 7.0's new LSP server
went GA July 8, 2026, superseding the plain-tsserver assumption; Python's `Pyrefly`/`ty` are
genuinely Rust-implemented but still subprocess/LSP-integrated, not embeddable libraries; Java's
`jdtls` import step hard-crashes via OOM past ~3000 files, a real gate requirement, not a graceful
degradation; Kotlin's `kotlin-lsp` is real but still built on the same unstable-per-JetBrains
foundation already flagged, just hidden behind a heavier IDE-embedding shell); and a confirmed,
structural gap in both LSP and SCIP — neither protocol carries a confidence field, so the
compilers' own internal degradation signals (Clang's `RecoveryExpr`, JDT's `isRecovered()`)
have to be recovered via a per-backend sentinel table, not trusted from protocol silence.

All 16 agents landed with real, verified findings. Here's the shape of it:

**The core design survived, but its return type didn't.** Every backend researched (9 languages deep, plus C#/Ruby/PHP) maps cleanly onto `PerCall`/`PerInvocation`/`Session` as a real cost ceiling — no language forced a fourth lifetime tier, which is good news for the architecture you sketched. But five independent per-language studies (Kotlin, Go, Scala, Rust, C++) converged, unprompted, on the same structural problem: real backends don't hand back "a precision tier to promote," they hand back candidate sets (Kotlin's `KaErrorCallInfo`), unreconciled dual algorithms (Go's confirmed-vs-candidate interface satisfaction), two independently-scored axes (Scala's Metals can give you the resolved implicit value without reliably explaining *why* it won), or genuinely new structured facts (Rust trait predicates, C++'s `RecoveryExpr`). Collapsing any of that into one enum bump would manufacture confidence the upstream tool never claimed — exactly the failure mode you were worried about.

Some standout findings:
- **TypeScript**: TS 7.0 (the native Go port) went **GA on July 8, 2026** — this is no longer speculative, and it changes the calculus: it's LSP-based, ships no embeddable API until 7.1, and `PerCall` is a non-starter for it (whole-program load dominates cost). `Session` is TS's *native* mode — VS Code never runs it any other way.
- **Python**: Pyrefly and `ty` are real, fast, Rust-*implemented* — but neither ships an embeddable Rust library. "Written in Rust" turned out not to mean "linkable into monokl's process."
- **Java**: `jdtls`'s OOM past ~3000 files is a hard crash, not a graceful slowdown — monokl needs an explicit project-size gate before ever attempting promotion, not "try and let it degrade."
- **Go/gopls**: never unifies its local (real) and global (fingerprint-approximated) interface-satisfaction checks — monokl shouldn't either.
- **Confidence signaling**: neither LSP nor SCIP has a confidence field, confirmed by direct spec inspection. The compilers *do* often know internally (Clang's `RecoveryExpr`, JDT's `isRecovered()`) — the protocol just throws it away. This needs a per-backend sentinel denylist, not a generic check.
- **Ruby's Sorbet** was the one real surprise: a compiled-in stdlib blob gives it near-zero fixed cold-start cost, making it the one backend where `PerCall` is actually cheap.

I've written the full design into a new **`docs/spec/06-daemon-architecture.md`** — the amended `PrecisionUpgrader` trait, the lifetime model (now nesting sub-resources and distinguishing owned-vs-attached, per the adversarial critiques), the `DaemonExtension` ingestion model (additive per-language payloads, following the SCIP/LSP/CodeQL precedent the research found), the confidence-signaling rules, and the full per-language table — linked from `README.md` and cross-referenced from `05-research-and-decisions.md` §14.

One thing I deliberately did **not** fold in this pass: the `LanguageId`/`capabilities()` trait signature fix (making them per-language rather than per-analyzer-instance, needed for §10's fallback tier to actually compile) touches ~10 real call sites across Parts 1 and 3 with real logic implications, not just a signature change — I don't want to rush that in as a drive-by inside an already-large response. Want me to do that as a focused follow-up next?

Is it possible to attache some level of confidence after the fact with the data that is returned? Think of it as enrichment of the AST data. We want our asystem to allow for that and to minimize required context when possible.

Shall we tackle the langID + capabilities now?

input.old_string: ## 6. Confidence-signaling rules
input.new_string:
## 5. Attaching confidence after the fact: the `PrecisionLedger`

§2's `UpgradeOutcome` is a *runtime* return value — what a `PrecisionUpgrader` hands back the
moment it's called. But nothing about this design should require confidence/enrichment to be
attached only at that moment, tied to the base analysis's own cache lifecycle. Three real cases
this needs to support cleanly:

- **Eager**: a `PrecisionUpgrader` runs inline during `analyze_with_profile`, same as §2 describes.
- **Lazy**: a query (`refs`/`definition`) needs higher precision than what's cached, and a backend
  happens to be available *right now* even though it wasn't at initial analysis time (a `Session`
  daemon started since, Clang got installed since) — enrichment happens at query time, without
  re-running or invalidating the base `FileAnalysis`.
- **Retroactive**: an explicit, separate pass (e.g. a future `monokl enrich` step, or an
  agent choosing to spend a turn on it) sweeps already-cached files and attaches confidence from
  whatever backends are available, entirely decoupled from when those files were originally
  analyzed.

All three need the same thing: confidence has to be **addressable and separately cacheable from
`FileAnalysis` itself**, not baked into it. Baking it in would mean every new confidence signal —
a `Session` becoming available, a new sentinel rule, a different upgrader version — forces a
rebuild of the (potentially large) base analysis blob it has nothing to do with, and conflates two
genuinely different invalidation lifecycles: `FileAnalysis` invalidates on content change;
confidence annotations invalidate on *backend availability or version* change, which can happen
without the file ever changing at all.

**Design: a `PrecisionLedger`, keyed by `ContentHash`, storing small, addressable annotations —
never a copy of the AST.** This mirrors the real precedent already found for exactly this shape:
LSP's diagnostics model (a list of `{range, severity, message, source}` tied to a document,
decoupled from the document's own content) and SCIP's `Occurrence` model (`{range, symbol,
symbol_roles}` — a thin annotation layer over source, not an embedded copy of it).

```rust
pub struct PrecisionAnnotation {
    /// Addressable pointer, not a copy — a span, a symbol identity, or an occurrence identity.
    pub target: AnnotationTarget,
    pub precision: CapabilityPrecision,
    /// "Exact via JDT full resolution" / "Structural via clangd, no compile_commands.json" —
    /// same provenance discipline as UpgradeOutcome (§2), CHA/RTA/points-to (§6 rule 5).
    pub provenance: &'static str,
    /// Which sentinel (if any) triggered a downgrade instead of a silent Exact claim — §6.
    pub sentinel: Option<SentinelKind>,
    /// The exact content this annotation applies to. A ContentHash mismatch means "stale,
    /// discard" with no further comparison needed — same invalidation key FileAnalysis's own
    /// disk cache already uses, just a separate store.
    pub for_content: ContentHash,
}

pub enum AnnotationTarget {
    Span { start: usize, end: usize },
    Symbol(SymbolId),
    Occurrence(OccurrenceId),
}

/// Separately persisted from FileAnalysis's own cache entry (its own section of
/// `.monokl/cache.json`, or its own file) — populated eagerly, lazily, or retroactively,
/// on its own invalidation schedule.
pub struct PrecisionLedger {
    by_content: FxHashMap<ContentHash, Vec<PrecisionAnnotation>>,
}
```

**Minimizing required context, concretely**: an annotation is a handful of small fields keyed by a
pointer, never the subtree or source text it applies to — a consumer resolves `target` against
data it already has (the base `FileAnalysis` it already fetched), rather than the annotation
carrying a redundant copy. This matters doubly for monokl specifically because of the existing
token-budget-aware output stage (Part 1, `budget.rs`, tiktoken o200k_base, 2MB cap): a compact
`provenance` tag travels with a result by default; the full reasoning behind it (which candidates
were considered, why a sentinel fired) is *not* inlined into every response — it's available on
demand through the `explain` command Part 2 already specifies, the natural place for a "why do you
believe this" drill-down that shouldn't tax every other query's budget. Default output stays terse;
depth is opt-in, not forced on every consumer.

This requires no change to §2's `PrecisionUpgrader` trait or §4's `DaemonExtension` — `UpgradeOutcome`
is exactly what gets turned into one or more `PrecisionAnnotation` entries when a ledger write
happens, whether that write is eager, lazy, or retroactive. The ledger is the addressing/storage
layer underneath, not a competing design.

input.prompt:
You're researching a design question for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below. Verify real papers/projects directly; don't recite from general impressions without checking.

## Background

monokl already has a categorical precision model: `CapabilityPrecision::{Unsupported, Heuristic, Structural, Exact}`. It also has a design (already built, don't re-research) for attaching this precision plus richer per-language facts to specific spans/symbols after the fact, via a `PrecisionAnnotation`/`PrecisionLedger` mechanism — separately cached, addressable by span/symbol, populated eagerly (during analysis), lazily (at query time), or retroactively (a later enrichment sweep). It also already has a design for detecting when an external tool (Clang, a language server) silently degraded rather than genuinely resolved something, via a "sentinel" denylist (known degraded-fallback patterns per backend — e.g. Clang's `RecoveryExpr`, Java's `IBinding.isRecovered()`).

The open question now: beyond that categorical, sentinel-based approach, is there real academic/research grounding for computing a more granular confidence signal — and if so, what does it actually look like in practice?

## What to research

1. **Probabilistic/ML-based type and fact inference for dynamically-typed or partially-typed code.** Verify these are real, get correct citations, and understand HOW each computes and calibrates a confidence value: DeepTyper (Hellendoorn, Bird, Barr, Allamanis — "Deep Learning Type Inference," ESEC/FSE 2018), TypeWriter (Pradel et al., "TypeWriter: Neural Type Prediction with Search-Based Validation," 2020), Type4Py (Mir et al., 2022), HiTyper, OptTyper, or any other real, citable system in this space. For each real one found: what signal does it actually predict confidence from (softmax probability from a neural model? something else?), and is there real discussion in these papers of calibration problems (a model's raw confidence score not matching its true accuracy rate — this is a well-known ML pitfall, verify whether these specific papers address it or not).
2. **"Naturalness of software" / statistical/n-gram code models as a lightweight, non-ML confidence signal.** Verify Hindle, Barr, Su, Gabel, Devanbu, "On the Naturalness of Software" (ICSE 2012) and its lineage — is there real, citable work using code's statistical regularities (n-gram language models over source, or similar) to flag low-probability/anomalous code as a confidence-relevant signal, distinct from a full neural type-inference model? How lightweight is this in practice (does it require training a model, or can simple corpus-frequency statistics work)?
3. **Ensemble/multi-tool agreement as a confidence signal.** Is there real research or documented industry practice on running multiple independent static analyzers/type-checkers over the same code and using their agreement/disagreement as a confidence signal (the static-analysis analog of ensemble methods in ML, or "N-version programming")? Look for real studies comparing multiple type checkers/analyzers on the same codebases and discussing agreement rates as a quality/confidence signal.
4. **Is there a real, lightweight, non-ML technique for combining multiple independent uncertain signals into one confidence value** — e.g., Dempster-Shafer evidence combination theory, simple Bayesian combination, or noisy-OR/noisy-AND style combinators — that's been applied to program analysis or verification specifically (not just generic ML/robotics contexts)? Real citation needed if so.
5. **Honest verdict**: given monokl's actual constraints (no training-data pipeline, no ML infrastructure, a lightweight Rust CLI tool, real-time query latency requirements), is a granular numeric confidence score even well-supported by this literature as worth building, or does the literature actually support staying categorical (the CHA/RTA/points-to-style discrete tiers monokl already has) as the more defensible, lower-risk choice? Don't force a "yes, build ML" answer if the evidence doesn't support it for monokl's specific constraints — say plainly if the categorical approach is actually the state-of-the-art-recommended choice for this kind of tool.

## Output

Real citations for every substantive claim (paper title, authors, venue/year — verify via search, don't recall from memory alone). End with a clear, honest recommendation: should monokl go beyond categorical precision tiers toward a computed numeric/probabilistic confidence score, and if so, what's the simplest real-evidence-backed technique to do it with (not requiring monokl to become an ML research project)? Target 700-1000 words.

You're researching a design question for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below. Verify real projects/docs/papers directly by fetching them; don't recite from general impressions without checking, since some of what you might "remember" about these tools' exact metadata fields could be wrong or outdated.

## Background

monokl already has a categorical precision model (`Unsupported/Heuristic/Structural/Exact`) and a design (already complete, don't re-research) for attaching precision plus richer facts to specific results after the fact, via a small addressable annotation store, tagged with which backend/operation produced each result ("Exact via JDT full resolution" vs. "Structural via clangd without a compilation database"). The open question: how do real, shipped static-analysis/code-intelligence tools actually handle confidence/precision as a concept in production, beyond monokl's own already-decided design?

## What to research

1. **CodeQL's query metadata.** Real CodeQL queries declare metadata tags in their `.ql` files — verify whether a `@precision` tag actually exists (checking real values like `very-high`/`high`/`medium`/`low` if so — don't guess the exact vocabulary, check real query files in github.com/github/codeql or its docs), what it's actually used for (is it purely documentation/query-selection guidance for security scanning tiers, or does it feed anything programmatic like alert filtering/ranking?), and whether it's a per-query (rule-level, set once by the query author) or per-finding (computed per instance) concept. This distinction matters a lot for monokl's design.
2. **Semgrep's rule metadata.** Verify whether Semgrep rules have a real `confidence` field in their YAML metadata (check real rule files or Semgrep's own rule-writing documentation at semgrep.dev), what values it takes, and how/whether it's actually surfaced to end users or used by tooling (e.g. does `semgrep ci`/Semgrep's own product filter or sort by it?).
3. **Facebook/Meta's static analysis deployment-at-scale practice.** Find and verify: Distefano, Fähndrich, Logozzo, O'Hearn, "Scaling Static Analyses at Facebook," Communications of the ACM, 2019 (or the closest real citation if this exact one doesn't check out) — this is reported to describe how Facebook's Infer/related tools use engineer accept/dismiss feedback signals over time to recalibrate which warnings actually get shown, i.e. a real, production feedback loop for confidence/precision tuning distinct from a fixed static rule. Verify the real mechanism described, not just the existence of the paper.
4. **Other real linters/static-analysis tools' confidence or false-positive-suppression practices** — SonarQube/SonarLint, ESLint, Pylint, or others — do any have a documented, real confidence-scoring or false-positive-suppression mechanism worth citing (e.g. historical-suppression learning, "this rule fires too often, deprioritize")?
5. **Honest synthesis**: across everything found, is per-instance numeric confidence scoring actually common in shipped, production static-analysis tooling today, or is the real, verified state of the art mostly *categorical, rule-author-declared* precision/severity tags (set once, not computed per finding) plus *separate, slower-moving* feedback loops (like Facebook's) that retune which categories of finding get shown over time — rather than a live per-instance score? Be honest about which pattern the evidence actually supports as dominant in real deployed tools.

## Output

Real citations (tool name, doc URL, or paper) for every substantive claim — flag clearly if you could not verify something you expected to find (e.g. if Semgrep's confidence field turns out not to be real, or CodeQL's precision tag works differently than commonly assumed). End with a concrete recommendation for monokl: which of these real patterns (rule-level precision tags, per-finding computed scores, slow feedback-loop retuning) is the most defensible one to adopt, and why. Target 600-900 words.

input.prompt:
You're researching a design question for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below. Verify real projects/crates directly; don't recite from general impressions.

## Background

monokl analyzes source statically — parsing ASTs (via OXC, `ra_ap_syntax`, tree-sitter, gosyn depending on language) and, where available, consulting real compilers/language servers for deeper resolution. It never executes the code it analyzes. The open question here: is there real, established practice for confirming or upgrading a statically-derived fact using a *dynamic/runtime* signal instead — i.e., confidence added "after the fact" from a genuinely different source than the AST or a static compiler pass — and separately, what concrete Rust-ecosystem tools/techniques exist for actually implementing a confidence combiner once multiple signals (static, sentinel-based, dynamic) need to be merged into one value?

## What to research

1. **MonkeyType** (Facebook/Instagram's real, open-source Python tool) — verify its real mechanism: does it use `sys.settrace`-style runtime tracing during actual test execution to record real argument/return types observed at runtime, then generate type stub annotations from that? How does it handle a function observed with multiple different real types across calls (union types, or does it pick a most-common one)? Does it expose or imply any notion of confidence based on how many times / how consistently a type was observed? This is real precedent for "confirm a static guess using a fundamentally different, dynamic signal source" — verify the actual mechanism from MonkeyType's own docs/repo (github.com/Instagram/MonkeyType), not from memory.
2. **Similar dynamic/runtime-tracing-based type or fact inference for other languages** — is there a real equivalent for JavaScript/TypeScript (dynamic type recording during test runs, e.g. anything used to auto-generate `.d.ts` files from runtime observation) or any other language monokl targets? Check for real, maintained projects, not abandoned experiments.
3. **Pytype's `reveal_type` and similar "ask the checker what it actually inferred" mechanisms** — is there real precedent for a static tool exposing its own confidence/certainty about an inferred fact directly (distinct from the sentinel-detection approach monokl already has, which infers degradation indirectly)?
4. **Concrete Rust crates for combining multiple uncertain/independent signals into one score.** Check crates.io directly for anything real and reasonably maintained implementing: (a) Dempster-Shafer evidence combination theory, (b) simple Bayesian/noisy-OR combinators, (c) any general "confidence/evidence combination" utility crate. Report real findings — if nothing suitable exists (which is plausible), say so plainly rather than stretching a tangential crate to fit.
5. **Given everything found across this research thread (and separately, two other research threads covering academic probabilistic-inference literature and industry tools' confidence practices — you don't have their findings, just be aware they exist), what's the simplest, most defensible concrete technique monokl could actually implement** for combining signals it already has available: (a) categorical precision tier from whichever analyzer/upgrader produced a result, (b) candidate-set size (1 = confident, N>1 = ambiguous), (c) sentinel-detected degradation (already designed), (d) potentially cross-tier agreement (native parser and daemon agree vs. disagree) — into something more useful than the raw categorical tier alone, without requiring monokl to build or ship any ML model or training pipeline? Favor simple, explainable, deterministic combination logic over anything requiring training data monokl doesn't have.

## Output

Real citations/sources for every substantive claim. End with a concrete, implementable recommendation scoped to what a lightweight Rust CLI tool can reasonably build and maintain — call out explicitly if the honest answer is "write this yourself, no library needed" for any part. Target 600-900 words.

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-confidence-runtime-impl" color="yellow" summary="Runtime-confirmation precedent + Rust combinator crates findings">
## 1. MonkeyType — verified against Instagram/MonkeyType source, not memory

Mechanism: uses `sys.setprofile` (a profiling hook, not `sys.settrace`) to interpose on function calls, returns, and generator yields during real test execution, recording the concrete types observed (github.com/Instagram/MonkeyType README).

Multi-type handling: in `monkeytype/stubs.py`, `shrink_traced_types()` collects every observed type per argument/return/yield across *all* traces into a set, then calls `shrink_types()` to reduce that set to a minimal-equivalent type — effectively a full union (e.g. collapsing to `Optional[X]` when `None` appears), not a "most common type" heuristic.

Confidence: none, explicitly. There is no frequency count, no "seen 95% of calls" score. The docs state annotations are "an informative first draft, to be checked and corrected by a developer" — the confidence mechanism is human review, not an automated score. This is real precedent for confirming a static guess with a *fundamentally different* signal source (execution rather than parsing), but it stops at "recording observed reality," it does not model confidence.

## 2. JS/TS equivalent

**TypeWiz** (github.com/urish/typewiz) is real and did exactly this — runtime monitoring during execution auto-annotates TS with observed types. But it's dead: last release Apr 2019, repo explicitly archived Oct 2021 with an owner note "as of 2021 I'm no longer working on TypeWiz." No actively maintained equivalent found. Treat as historical precedent only, not a tool to integrate with or model implementation details on.

## 3. pytype `reveal_type`

Confirmed real by reading pytype's own source (not docs, which don't mention it): `pytype/overlays/typing_overlay.py` registers `reveal_type`, backed by `RevealType` in `pytype/overlays/special_builtins.py`. Its `call()` does exactly one thing: `self.ctx.errorlog.reveal_type(...)` — prints the inferred type, mirroring mypy's `reveal_type`. No confidence/certainty field attached. So: no precedent, anywhere I could verify, for a static checker exposing a *confidence score* distinct from the type itself via this mechanism — `reveal_type` conventions across the ecosystem (mypy, pyright, pytype) all just answer "what type," never "how sure." This actually strengthens the case that monokl's sentinel-based indirect degradation approach is already ahead of common practice, not behind it.

## 4. Rust crates for combining signals — direct crates.io API checks

- **Dempster-Shafer**: `furtif-core` is real and does implement belief-function fusion (`EnumRule::DempsterShafer` in its examples), part of the `silx-furtif` monorepo (LGPL-3.0). But it's essentially abandoned: 2 GitHub stars, 1 fork, 5 total commits, last updated March 2024, only 16 recent downloads against 5,573 lifetime (a one-time burst, not ongoing use). Not viable as a dependency.
- **Bayesian**: the `bayesian` crate is real but is a naive-Bayes *text classifier* (with TF-IDF), not a general evidence-combinator — wrong shape for merging independent confidence signals.
- **General combinator utility**: nothing suitable. Note: crates.io's search API backfills low-relevance queries with unrelated popular/trending crates (verified directly — a TUI library, FrankenTUI, appeared identically across unrelated queries like "evidence combination" and "bayesian"); I had to filter those out by checking real relevance per hit. Beyond the fillers, the only genuine hits were ultra-niche and off-target: `flux-perception` ("confidence-weighted sensor fusion for autonomous agents," 15 downloads, one month old, unproven) and `tracktor`/`multisensor-lmb-filters-rs` (Random Finite Set / Labeled Multi-Bernoulli filters — real techniques, but for radar/robotics multi-object tracking, a different problem shape entirely).
- **Bottom line**: no mature, general-purpose Rust crate exists for this. This part is genuinely "write it yourself."

## 5. Recommendation

Don't reach for Dempster-Shafer or Bayesian combination — both require inputs monokl doesn't have (mass assignments over a frame of discernment, or calibrated priors/likelihoods from training data). Given only categorical tier, candidate-set size, sentinel-degradation, and cross-tier agreement, the defensible approach is a small **deterministic ordinal downgrade lattice**, not a numeric probability:

- Start from the categorical tier as the baseline (already the primary signal).
- Each secondary signal can only *downgrade* confidence one step, never algorithmically upgrade it — this avoids manufacturing false precision from what are really just fewer red flags, not more positive evidence. `candidate_set_size > 1` → downgrade one level (ambiguous); sentinel-degradation detected → downgrade one level.
- The one signal allowed to counteract a downgrade is genuine cross-tier agreement (two independently-derived analyzers concurring) — that's authentic corroboration from a different source, structurally the same kind of "confirm with a different signal" precedent MonkeyType embodies, just applied deterministically instead of via observed-frequency.
- Implement as a small enum + explicit combination function (~50-100 lines, unit-testable), explainable directly in `michi`-formatted output (e.g. "high, downgraded: ambiguous candidate set"). No library needed for any part of this.

All citations below verified directly (arXiv/DBLP/ACM/PDF full-text), not recalled from memory alone.

## 1. ML-based type/fact inference — confidence signal & calibration

- **DeepTyper** (Hellendoorn, Bird, Barr, Allamanis, "Deep Learning Type Inference," ESEC/FSE 2018, DOI 10.1145/3236024.3236051) — REAL, verified via full-text PDF. Confidence = raw softmax probability of the top RNN prediction (Eq. 1 in paper: `P(τ) = softmax(...)`). Used directly as a precision/recall threshold: paper's own numbers show a 90% confidence threshold yields only ~80% precision, and a 99% threshold yields ~95% precision (Fig. 5). That gap (0.90 stated confidence → 0.80 actual correctness) is a textbook calibration gap — but the paper never uses the word "calibration" and does no reliability-diagram/ECE/Brier analysis. It's an unexamined side effect visible only in their raw results table.
- **TypeWriter** (Pradel, Gousios, Liu, Chandra, arXiv 1912.03768 / ESEC-FSE 2020) — REAL. Notably does NOT lean on model confidence at all — it validates predictions by round-tripping candidate types through a real gradual type checker and search, i.e. confidence is established by an independent symbolic oracle, not trusted from the model.
- **Type4Py** (Mir, Latoskinas, Proksch, Gousios, ICSE 2022) — REAL. Uses nearest-neighbor similarity ranking (MRR), not a calibrated probability at all.
- **HiTyper** (Peng, Gao, Li, Gao, Lo, Zhang, Lyu, ICSE 2022) — REAL. Hybrid: static "type rejection rules" filter/veto neural predictions rather than trusting a confidence score.
- **OptTyper** (Vlassi Pandi, Barr, Gordon, Sutton, arXiv 2004.00348) — REAL (note: 4th author is Charles Sutton, not Lahiri). Combines hard logical constraints from a real type system with a learned "natural" signal via continuous optimization — again, a symbolic check gates the statistical one.

**Pattern across all five:** none does formal calibration analysis, and every single one that ships a real system pairs the statistical signal with an independent symbolic validator rather than trusting raw model confidence. That validator-gates-model pattern is structurally identical to what monokl's sentinel/categorical design already does.

## 2. Naturalness of software (lightweight, non-ML)

**Hindle, Barr, Gabel, Su, Devanbu, "On the Naturalness of Software," ICSE 2012 (CACM 59(5) reprint 2016, DOI 10.1145/2902362)** — REAL, verified via full-text. Core method: plain n-gram MLE frequency counting over a code corpus (no neural net, no training pipeline — literally token co-occurrence counting), scored via cross-entropy/perplexity. This is genuinely lightweight — could run over monokl's own indexed corpus. Lineage confirmed: **Ray, Hellendoorn, Godhane, Tu, Bacchelli, Devanbu, "On the 'Naturalness' of Buggy Code," ICSE 2016** (DBLP-verified) empirically shows buggy lines score measurably less "natural" (higher entropy) than clean code — a real, direct precedent for using a statistical anomaly score as a confidence-adjacent signal, entirely apart from any ML type-inference model.

## 3. Ensemble/multi-tool agreement

**Habib & Pradel, "How Many of All Bugs Do We Find? A Study of Static Bug Detectors," ASE 2018** (DBLP-verified, DOI 10.1145/3238147.3238213) and **Lenarduzzi, Pecorelli, Saarimäki, Lujan, Palomba, "A Critical Comparison on Six Static Analysis Tools," JSS 2023** (DBLP-verified) — both REAL. Both found LOW agreement/overlap between independent static analyzers on real code — tools mostly find disjoint issue sets. This actually argues against naive "multi-tool agreement = confidence" reasoning: absence of agreement is the norm even among sound analyzers, so agreement can't be treated as a reliable confidence multiplier without a lot more calibration work of its own.

## 4. Bayesian/lightweight combination specifically for program analysis

Did NOT find real Dempster-Shafer work specifically applied to program analysis/verification — the DS papers I found were generic (not program-analysis-specific), so don't claim that citation. What IS real and directly on point:
- **Kremenek & Engler, "Z-Ranking: Using Statistical Analysis to Counter the Impact of Static Analysis Approximations," SAS 2003** — REAL. Simple frequency/z-score statistical model ranking static-analysis error reports by true-positive likelihood, no ML training required.
- **Kremenek, Ashcraft, Yang, Engler, "Correlation Exploitation in Error Ranking," FSE 2004** (DOI 10.1145/1029894.1029909) — REAL. Uses Bayesian factor graphs + belief propagation to combine multiple correlated static-analysis signals into one ranking/confidence value. This is the best real precedent for "combine several independent uncertain signals into one number, for program analysis specifically" — and it's 20+ years old, lightweight, no deep learning.

- Multi-tool agreement is empirically *rare even among correct analyzers* (two separate verified studies) — so cross-tier agreement is real corroboration when it happens, but its absence isn't a red flag and shouldn't be over-weighted.
- Every real shipped tool checked (CodeQL's `@precision`, Semgrep's `confidence`) uses **categorical, rule-author-declared tags** — exactly what `CapabilityPrecision` already is — never a live per-finding score.

**Concrete recommendation, converging all three threads**: keep `CapabilityPrecision` categorical (already right). Compute per-result precision via a small deterministic **ordinal downgrade lattice** — start from the categorical tier, let ambiguous candidate sets and sentinel hits each downgrade one step, let genuine cross-tier agreement counteract one downgrade (real signal, just not a strong one) — no numeric score, ~50-100 lines, unit-testable. Separately, add a Tricorder-style slow feedback loop: track a reliability ratio per `(backend, operation)` pair over time (not per-finding), and let a chronically-unreliable combination get systematically down-weighted — the one long-term-learning mechanism with genuine production precedent. ## 7. Computing precision: sourcing, the downgrade lattice, and long-term feedback

§5-6 establish where confidence lives (the `PrecisionLedger`) and how to detect degradation
(sentinels). This section answers the question underneath both: what actually produces a
`PrecisionAnnotation`'s value, and how much of that should be genuinely new machinery vs. combining
signals monokl already has. Grounded in a dedicated research pass across academic literature,
real shipped tools, and runtime/implementation options — not designed in the abstract.

**Where each signal actually comes from:**

- **From the AST/parse itself, at analysis time**: the base categorical tier
  (`Heuristic`/`Structural`/`Exact`) a `LanguageAnalyzer` or `PrecisionUpgrader` reports, and
  candidate-set size — 1 resolved candidate vs. N ambiguous ones is a structural fact straight out
  of the symbol table, not an inference.
- **After the fact, at query time or later**: sentinel-detected degradation (§6 — consulting an
  external tool's raw output for known fallback markers), cross-tier agreement (comparing two
  independently-derived answers for the same fact, e.g. a native parser's heuristic guess and a
  daemon's real resolution), and — optionally, not required for v1 — a slow-moving,
  usage-derived reliability signal per `(backend, operation)` pair gathered across many runs (see
  Tricorder below). This is exactly why §5 designed the ledger as separately addressable and
  separately invalidated from `FileAnalysis`: none of these after-the-fact signals should require
  re-running or invalidating the base analysis to attach.

**What the state of the art says not to build.** Every real ML-based type/fact-inference system
checked (DeepTyper, TypeWriter, Type4Py, HiTyper, OptTyper — all verified directly, not recalled)
either skips calibration analysis entirely or, examined against its own published numbers, shows a
real gap between stated confidence and actual accuracy (DeepTyper's own results: a 90%-confidence
threshold yields only ~80% true precision). And — the load-bearing finding — every one of these
systems, without exception, still pairs its statistical signal with an independent symbolic
validator rather than trusting the model's raw confidence (TypeWriter round-trips candidates
through a real type checker; HiTyper uses static rejection rules to veto neural predictions).
That validator-gates-model pattern is structurally identical to what §6's sentinel design already
is — the literature confirms monokl's existing approach rather than pointing toward a trained
model. Separately, two real studies (Habib & Pradel, "How Many of All Bugs Do We Find?", ASE 2018;
Lenarduzzi et al., "A Critical Comparison on Six Static Analysis Tools," JSS 2023) found that
agreement between independent static analyzers is empirically rare *even among analyzers that are
each individually correct* — so cross-tier agreement is real corroboration when observed, but its
*absence* is the normal case and must not be scored as a red flag.

Real, shipped, production tools converge on the same categorical answer. CodeQL's `@precision` tag
(verified directly against its metadata docs) takes exactly four values — `low`/`medium`/`high`/
`very-high` — set once by the query author, feeding only display, never a per-finding computation.
Semgrep's rule metadata has a real `confidence` field (`HIGH`/`MEDIUM`/`LOW`, verified against real
shipped rules), used to curate which rules run in CI-blocking vs. audit-only mode — again rule-level,
not per-instance. **Google's Tricorder is the one fully-verified, real production feedback
mechanism** (Sadowski et al., "Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google," CACM 2018,
full text read directly): every finding shown in code review carries a "Please fix"/"Not useful"
button, the ratio is tracked *per analyzer*, and an analyzer that crosses a 10% not-useful rate gets
disabled until its authors improve it — categorical, slow-moving, tuned at the analyzer/rule level,
never a live per-instance score. Across every real tool checked, there is zero evidence of a
production system attaching a live numeric confidence value to individual findings.

**Concrete design: an ordinal downgrade lattice, not a numeric score.** `PrecisionAnnotation.precision`
is computed by starting from the categorical tier the producing analyzer/upgrader already reports,
then applying secondary signals that can only ever move it *down* one step, never up:

```rust
fn compute_precision(
    reported: CapabilityPrecision,
    candidates: &[UpgradeCandidate],
    sentinel: Option<SentinelKind>,
    cross_tier_agreement: bool,
) -> CapabilityPrecision {
    let mut precision = reported;
    if candidates.len() > 1 { precision = precision.saturating_downgrade(); }
    if sentinel.is_some() { precision = precision.saturating_downgrade(); }
    // Real corroboration when present — but per the agreement-is-rare finding above, this
    // counteracts at most one downgrade step. It is never grounds to exceed `reported`.
    if cross_tier_agreement && precision < reported {
        precision = precision.saturating_upgrade().min(reported);
    }
    precision
}
```

No numeric probability anywhere — the output stays one of the same four `CapabilityPrecision`
values already shown to agents today, so nothing about existing output formats or the token-budget
discipline changes. This is a small, deterministic, unit-testable function (no training data, no
model, no new dependency — a real, checked absence: no viable Rust crate exists for combining
uncertain signals; the one real Dempster-Shafer crate found is effectively abandoned, and the
"bayesian" crate on crates.io is a text classifier, the wrong shape entirely). The closest real
academic precedent for this class of combination, done for program analysis specifically rather
than borrowed from an unrelated ML domain, is Kremenek & Engler's Z-Ranking (SAS 2003) and its
follow-up "Correlation Exploitation in Error Ranking" (Kremenek, Ashcraft, Yang, Engler, FSE 2004)
— simple statistical combination of correlated analysis signals into a ranking, over 20 years old,
no deep learning required.

**Optional, real, not required for v1**: n-gram "naturalness" scoring (Hindle, Barr, Gabel, Su,
Devanbu, "On the Naturalness of Software," ICSE 2012/CACM 2016) is a genuinely lightweight
additional signal — plain corpus frequency counting, no training pipeline — and its lineage (Ray et
al., "On the 'Naturalness' of Buggy Code," ICSE 2016) shows buggy code measurably scores less
"natural" (higher cross-entropy) than clean code. If ever wanted, this could feed
`compute_precision` as one more downgrade signal (statistically anomalous code relative to monokl's
own indexed corpus → one more reason to downgrade), computed over data monokl already indexes, with
no dependency on any daemon or external tool. Not committed to now — flagged as a real, citable,
low-cost option if finer-grained downgrading is ever wanted.

**Optional long-term feedback loop, modeled directly on Tricorder**: track a reliability ratio per
`(backend, operation)` pair — e.g. "Structural via clangd without a compilation database" —
across many runs, and let a combination that proves chronically unreliable get systematically
down-weighted (an extra forced downgrade step, or excluded from `Exact` promotion entirely until
revisited). This requires a feedback signal monokl doesn't have designed yet (something analogous
to Tricorder's "Please fix"/"Not useful" click — plausibly an agent or user later confirming/
correcting a specific annotation) and is explicitly not part of the v1 design; it's recorded here
because it's the one mechanism with genuine, fully-verified production precedent for improving
precision *over time* rather than per-query, and the `(backend, operation)`-keyed granularity
already matches `PrecisionAnnotation.provenance` (§5) exactly, so no new identifier scheme would be
needed if it's ever built.

That BFS should adopt the same hardening codegraph's own `GraphTraverser` needed in production: an `FxHashSet<FileIdx>` visited-set checked at enqueue time (not just dequeue), an explicit depth limit, and a result cap checked at every push site rather than only the loop head. Surface a cap-hit as a first-class, matchable outcome — extend `MonoklError` with a non-fatal `TraversalCapExceeded { visited: usize, cap: usize }` variant, returned inside a `TraversalReport { sites: Vec<_>, truncated: bool }` rather than silently truncating a bare `Vec`. The same bounded-BFS pattern generalizes to any of this spec's existing traversals (`dependents`/`imports_of`, impact-radius-style queries) that don't yet have explicit cap enforcement at every site.
- **Generalize `TraitImplIndex` toward SCIP's `Relationship` shape, not its wire format** (full research in §7). Tag each `(FileIdx, usize)` entry with which relationship kind it represents (`is_implementation`/`is_type_definition`/`is_reference`/`is_definition`, mirroring `scip.proto`'s `Relationship` message) instead of assuming "implementation" for everything — free forward-compatibility for non-trait-impl relationships later, at no cost now. Do not adopt SCIP's symbol-moniker grammar as a `FileIdx` replacement, and do not treat rust-analyzer's own SCIP output as a source of this data today — its CLI hardcodes `relationships: Vec::new()` as of this research pass (verified against `crates/rust-analyzer/src/cli/scip.rs`), so the one crate that could plausibly supply this for free currently supplies nothing.
- **An RTA-style instantiation filter over `TraitImplIndex`** (literature grounding in §8) — cross-reference implementor types against observed struct-literal/constructor sites already collected by `SymbolIndex`, pruning "declared-hierarchy" hits down to "declared and actually constructed" ones. Same cost order as the existing CHA-shaped pass already described above; a real precision improvement, not a new `CapabilityPrecision` tier.
- **Optional `.scip` file ingestion as a precision-upgrade path, not a dependency** (§7). If a `.scip` index already exists in-repo (produced out-of-band by `scip-typescript`/`scip-java`/ `rust-analyzer scip`), an optional reader via the official `scip` crate (v0.9.0, one real dependency, `protobuf = "=3.7.2"`) could promote matching occurrences from `Heuristic`/ `Structural` to `Exact`. Never invoked live, never required — a batch precompute a user opts into, not a monokl dependency.
- **A `MatchStrictness`-style spectrum for the query pipeline's structural-evaluation stage** (§7), modeled on ast-grep's `Cst/Smart/Ast/Relaxed/Signature/Template` dial — lets a query relax from "match kind, text, and trivia" down to "match kind only" without falling all the way back to plain text search. Pair with ast-grep's relational-rule vocabulary (`inside`/`has`/`follows`/ `precedes`, each with a `stopBy` of immediate-neighbor/until-end/until-a-rule, plus field-targeted matching via `child_by_field_id`) for the `patterns`/`schema` command family (Part 2) — a composable primitive for "structural pattern within structural context" that's a real step up from kind+text matching alone.
- **A content-hash-based move detector for the `diff` command** (§7) — hash each named top-level declaration by normalized subtree content and match across the two trees by hash before doing any positional diffing. Cheap, and difftastic — the most mature tree-sitter-based structural differ surveyed — still doesn't have this (`Wilfred/difftastic#508`, opened 2023, unimplemented) — a real edge over the strongest prior art examined. Also adopt difftastic's per-language `atom_nodes`/`delimiter_tokens`-equivalent config (which node kinds are leaves for diff purposes, which delimiters pair) — monokl's tree-sitter-backed analyzers (Python, Java) will hit the same false-diff bugs without it.
- **A generic tree-sitter fallback tier, launching with C, C++, Bash, and C#** (full research in §10). One `LanguageAnalyzer` impl handling all four via a small internal per-language config table, `Heuristic`/`Structural`-only, no bespoke `InspectEntry` classifier per language — same one-impl-per-language shape `AnalyzerRegistry` already dispatches on, just with that one impl owning N languages instead of one. C++ launches capped at `Heuristic` specifically (not `Structural`) given a real, currently-unresolved grammar ambiguity in `tree-sitter-cpp` (statement parsing is expression-vs-declaration-ambiguous without type info the parser never sees). `CapabilityPrecision` must be reported per-language-instance inside this one analyzer, not per-impl — the existing five analyzers never needed this since each already owns exactly one language.

< # Architecture This is the design in prose. For verbatim code, see [`docs/spec/`](docs/spec/README.md). ## Two levels: analyze once, aggregate separately Every file gets parsed exactly once, by a `LanguageAnalyzer`: ``` file → LanguageAnalyzer::analyze() → FileAnalysis (owned: symbols, deps, exports, code blocks) ``` `FileAnalysis` never borrows from the parser's arena — everything in it is owned data (`String`, not `&str`; `Vec<T>` of owned items). The arena drops at the end of `analyze()`. This is a hard rule, not a style preference: it's what lets `FileAnalysis` be cached, shared across threads via `Arc`, and outlive the parse call that produced it. A second layer, `WorkspaceEnricher`, folds per-file analyses into workspace-wide structure — an import graph, a symbol index — without re-parsing anything: ``` Vec<FileAnalysis> → WorkspaceEnricher::update() × N files → WorkspaceIndex ``` Two enrichers exist today: `ImportGraphEnricher` (which files import which) and `SymbolIndexEnricher` (symbol name → declaration sites). Both are cheap bookkeeping over already-parsed data — the expensive part is parsing, done once, upstream. Building a `WorkspaceIndex` is three phases: 1. **Parallel analyze.** Walk the directory, run `LanguageAnalyzer::analyze()` per file via `rayon`, then sort by path — sorting *after* parallel completion, not enforcing commit order *during* it, because import resolution is real (`oxc_resolver`, not name-matching), so there's no candidate-disambiguation-by-insertion-order problem to solve in the first place. 2. **Stream `update()`** for every (file, enricher) pair. 3. **`finalize()`** each enricher — by now the full file index exists, so an enricher can resolve `Utf8PathBuf → FileIdx` for edges it deferred during `update()`. ## The search pipeline `search` is eight stages, each one doing strictly less work on strictly fewer candidates than the last: 1. Parse the query (`+required` / `-excluded` / bare-optional / `"phrase"` / `regex:pattern`). 2. Canonicalize the workspace root. 3. Text prefilter — `grep-searcher` (the crate ripgrep is built on) over the candidate file set. 4. Boolean evaluation — drop files missing a required term or containing an excluded one. 5. Block retrieval — analyze surviving files, keep only code blocks overlapping a matched line. 6. BM25 rank (`K1=1.5`, `B=0.5`) plus a node-type boost (functions rank higher than modules) and a coverage boost (more of the block matched = higher). 7. Dedup — drop blocks that overlap >50% with a higher-ranked block in the same file. 8. Token budget — truncate to fit, with an explicit marker so an agent knows results were cut. Every stage is designed to fail toward "fewer, better results" rather than "more results, sort it out downstream" — the token budget in stage 8 is a last resort, not the primary filter. ## Caching: two tiers, one invariant ``` stat(path) → mtime + size match? → return cached, no file read → no match → read file → blake3 hash → hash match? → refresh mtime, return cached → no match → re-parse, cache result ``` `ContentHash` (blake3) is authoritative; mtime/size is the cheap dirty-bit that avoids reading files that haven't actually changed. Two storage layers: an in-memory `DashMap` (process-local, lock-free reads) for repeat calls within one run, and a disk-persisted `.monokl/cache.json` (version- and config-hash-gated, so a monokl upgrade or a tsconfig change invalidates it automatically) for repeat calls across separate CLI invocations. There's deliberately no persistent on-disk *search* index (no tantivy-style inverted index, no SQLite). The cache remembers *parses*; the `WorkspaceIndex` (import graph, symbol index) is rebuilt in memory on every invocation from the cached per-file data — cheap, because it's aggregation over already-parsed structure, not re-parsing. See [`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md) for the numbers behind that tradeoff and when it stops holding (roughly: past ~50k files, a persistent session becomes worth its complexity — not decided yet, tracked as an open question). ## Multi-language: capability, not uniformity Not every language gets the same precision, and the design says so explicitly instead of pretending otherwise. Every analyzer reports a `CapabilityPrecision` per operation: ``` Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact ``` - **Exact** — real resolution (e.g. TS/JS import resolution via `oxc_resolver`). - **Structural** — real AST parsing, heuristic resolution (Rust's module-path walker; Go's `go.mod`-based cross-package resolution). - **Heuristic** — regex/text-scan level (a language with no real parser yet). - **Unsupported** — the operation doesn't exist for this language. When an operation asks for more precision than an analyzer can give, the response carries a `Skipped` or `Warning` diagnostic instead of silently returning wrong answers or crashing. An `AnalyzerRegistry` dispatches each file to the first analyzer that claims it — TS/JS and Rust are registered with full native parsers; Python, Go, and Java are specified at `Structural` target precision but not yet implemented (see [README.md](README.md) for current status). ## What's explicitly out of scope Full list and rationale in [PRINCIPLES.md](PRINCIPLES.md#non-goals) — briefly: no persistent search index, no full [Salsa](https://github.com/salsa-rs/salsa) incremental framework (yet — tracked as an open investigation, not ruled out), no embedding-based retrieval by default, no stemming, no in-memory trigram index (measured at 600MB–1.2GB at scale in an earlier design, rejected for cause).
